title: First exchange
verifiedBy: Fable (Claude Fable 5) — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: A yes/no question is the statement, unchanged, with hal in front: anta min al-Hind → hal anta min al-Hind? Nothing moves and nothing is added at the end. English fronts an auxiliary ("are you", "do you") that Arabic simply does not have.

There are two words for "you", and they split by GENDER, not by politeness: anta to a man, anti to a woman. English has one word for both, so every question you ask now forces a choice English never made you make. (The plural antum is out of L1.)
"How are you?" is kayfa ḥāluka — "how (is) your state". No verb, exactly as in M1, and the "your" is the same kind of suffix as the -ī of ismī: ḥāluka to a man, ḥāluki to a woman.

al- changes shape before about half the letters of the alphabet — the sun letters — and this course WRITES the change: as-salām (not al-salām), ash-shāy (not al-shāy). Before the other half it stays plain: al-khayr, al-qahwa, al-Hind. The l is what disappears; the following letter doubles.
bi- is a small word glued onto the front of a noun, "with" or "in": bi-khayr is literally "in goodness", which is how Arabic says "fine". M8 uses the same bi- to ask a price.

The greetings come in fixed pairs — as-salāmu ʿalaykum is answered with wa ʿalaykum as-salām, and ṣabāḥ al-khayr with ṣabāḥ an-nūr. The reply is not a translation of the greeting; it is its own set phrase.

naʿam and lā stand alone and then the whole statement follows: naʿam, anā min al-Hind. English can stop at "Yes, I am" because "am" is a word; Arabic has no such word to stop on, so the answer repeats the sentence.

The -a that marks something as feminine follows the SUBJECT — the person the sentence is about, never the person saying it: hal anti ṭāliba? is asked OF a woman, whoever is asking. A man answering the same question says anā ṭālib.

words.note: The greeting of the whole Arabic-speaking world, learned as one piece. Inside it: salām is peace, and as- is the article al- with its l swallowed by the s that follows — a sun letter, written the way it is said. The -u on salāmu is a frozen ending this phrase keeps and nothing else in L1 does.

sentences.trap: It is not "peace upon you" as a sentence you could build words into. It is one fixed greeting, and it has one fixed answer.
sentences.sound: as-sa-LAA-mu ʿa-LAY-kum. The ʿ is a squeeze deep in the throat, not a vowel.

variations.changed: a plain hello — shorter, and no fixed reply is attached to it
the one fixed answer — the halves swap and wa opens the reply

mistake.why: That is the shape of the REPLY, and the reply also needs wa in front: wa ʿalaykum as-salām. The greeting itself is as-salāmu ʿalaykum.

sentences.usage: Any first meeting, spoken or written, formal or not. It is the safest greeting there is.
sentences.mnemonic: salām is the same word as the Hebrew shalom, and it means peace.

words.note: ʿalā ("upon") with the ending -kum ("you", plural) welded on — a preposition carrying its pronoun inside it, the way M1's ismī carried "my". The plural is used to one person here out of courtesy.
salām (peace) with the article. Written as- and not al- because s is a sun letter: the l assimilates, and this course writes what is said.

sentences.trap: The two halves swap places in the reply — and the wa is not optional.
sentences.sound: wa-ʿa-LAY-kum as-sa-LAAM — one run, no pause after wa.

variations.changed: drop as-salām — the everyday shortcut between people who know each other

variations.cue: And upon you, peace — how are you? (to a man)
variations.changed: the reply flows straight into the next question — one breath, two moves of the exchange

mistake.why: The reply starts with wa, "and" — "and upon YOU, peace". Without it, it sounds like a greeting said backwards.

sentences.usage: The answer to as-salāmu ʿalaykum, and the only answer. Never left unsaid.
sentences.mnemonic: The greeting gives peace; the reply gives it back — with an "and" on the front.

words.note: Two nouns stacked, not an adjective on a noun: ṣabāḥ is morning and khayr is goodness, so it says "morning of the goodness". Here al- keeps its l, because kh is a moon letter — compare as-salām, where s swallowed it. Swap the time noun and the frame holds: masāʾ al-khayr, good evening — al-khayr never changes.

sentences.trap: "Good" is not an adjective here. You cannot swap another adjective in: the phrase is fixed.
sentences.sound: ṣa-BAAḤ al-KHAYR. ṣ is a heavy s with the tongue low, and kh is the ch of Scottish "loch".

variations.changed: morning → evening; al-khayr never changes
the fixed answer — "morning of light", and n is another sun letter

variations.cue: Good morning — how are you? (to a man)
variations.changed: the greeting opens the exchange: kayfa ḥāluka follows in the same breath

mistake.why: The article is part of the phrase: ṣabāḥ al-khayr. Without it the words are just "morning" and "goodness" side by side.

sentences.usage: Until about noon; masāʾ al-khayr takes over for the rest of the day. In speech the name usually gets a yā in front of it — ṣabāḥ al-khayr yā Rohān — and the bare name is what writing looks like.
sentences.mnemonic: You are not wishing a good morning, you are handing over "the morning of goodness".

words.note: "How", and it goes first, exactly where English puts it.
ḥāl is a state or condition; -ka is "your" to a man and -ki "your" to a woman — the same suffix machinery as M1's ismī / ismuka / ismuki. There is no verb in the question at all.

sentences.trap: English asks with a verb ("how ARE you"). Arabic asks with two nouns and no verb, and the "you" is not even a word — it is the tail of ḥāl.
sentences.sound: KAY-fa ḤAA-lu-ka — ḥ is the hard breathy h, as in uḥibb.

variations.changed: -ka → -ki: the ending picks the person you are speaking to
the how-question turned yes/no: hal in front of the plain statement
the answer: naʿam, then the whole statement — there is no "am" to stop on

mistake.why: ḥāl on its own is just "state". The question needs the "your" welded on: kayfa ḥāluka / kayfa ḥāluki.

sentences.usage: Understood everywhere and slightly bookish out loud — Cairo says izzayyak, Damascus kīfak. This course stays with the written standard.
sentences.mnemonic: ḥāl is your state of affairs — asking "how is your ḥāl" is asking how things stand.

words.note: bi- is a one-letter word for "with" or "in", written onto the front of its noun: bi-khayr = "in goodness" = fine. The same bi- turns up in M8's bi-kam ("for how much"). And again there is no verb: anā bi-khayr is the whole answer.
"Thanks", with the same -an tail as M1's kathīran. One word, any situation.

sentences.trap: There is no "am" to translate, and no "you" in the thanks — both are one word shorter than English.
sentences.sound: bi-KHAYR runs as one word. shukran ends -an: SHUK-ran.

variations.changed: drop shukran — the answer alone is complete
a name instead of anā, and still nothing where "is" would be

variations.cue: I am fine — and you? (to a man)
variations.changed: wa anta? hands the question back — two words, and the exchange turns around

mistake.why: Without bi- this says "I am goodness". The little bi- is what makes it "in good shape": anā bi-khayr.

sentences.usage: The standard answer to kayfa ḥāluka, whether or not it is true.
sentences.mnemonic: bi-khayr = "in good" — you are inside the goodness.

sentences.cue: Are you from India? (to a man)

words.note: A question word with no English translation: put it in front of any statement and the statement becomes a yes/no question. It never changes, and nothing else in the sentence moves. In speech people often just raise the voice instead; hal is what gets written.
"You" said to a man. A woman is anti — Arabic has no single word covering both, so every "you" is a choice. Like anā, it is obligatory here because the sentence has no verb.

sentences.trap: English turns the sentence around to ask ("you are" → "are you"). Arabic leaves it exactly as it stands and puts hal in front.
sentences.sound: hal is short, flat and unstressed: hal AN-ta min al-HIND.

variations.cue: Are you a student? (to a man)
variations.changed: swap what is being asked about — hal anta holds still
drop hal and it is a plain statement again

variations.cue: Are you from India? (to a woman)
variations.changed: anta → anti: the same question, turned to a woman

mistake.why: English "are you…" wants a verb, so learners reach for one. The present has none: hal + the plain statement, hal anta min al-Hind?

sentences.usage: Everyday asking. hal fronts any statement you can already make.
sentences.mnemonic: hal is a question mark you say out loud, and it goes at the front.

words.note: "Yes", standing on its own before the answer. The ʿ in the middle is the throat-squeeze, so it is na-ʿam, two beats.

sentences.trap: "Yes, I am" cannot be translated — there is no "am" to end on. The answer says the whole thing again.
sentences.sound: na-ʿAM, with the throat catch between the two syllables.

variations.changed: same yes, a different statement behind it
the statement behind naʿam can be a verb sentence — the u- already carries the I
answering for someone else: a name in the subject slot, and still no verb

mistake.why: This is just "yes, I". With no verb "to be" to lean on, the answer has to repeat the statement: naʿam, anā min al-Hind.

sentences.usage: Answering any hal question. Short, and then the fact.
sentences.mnemonic: naʿam has the ʿayn in it — say yes from the throat.

sentences.cue: Are you a student? (to a woman)

words.note: "You" said to a woman — one letter away from anta and never interchangeable with it. In Arabic script the two look identical unless the vowel is marked, so the choice is heard rather than seen.

sentences.trap: Both halves move together: anti brings ṭāliba with it. Mixing them — anti ṭālib — is the commonest beginner slip.
sentences.sound: AN-ti TAA-li-ba. The final -a of ṭāliba is short and light.

variations.cue: Are you a student? (to a man)
variations.changed: anti → anta, and ṭāliba loses its -a to match

variations.cue: Yes, I am a student (said by a woman)
variations.changed: her answer: naʿam, and ṭāliba keeps its -a — the subject is still a woman
the anti chain runs through adjectives too: saʿīda follows her the way ṭāliba did

mistake.why: ṭālib describes a man. Asked of a woman, the word for student is ṭāliba — the ending follows the person the question is about.

sentences.usage: Asking someone what they do. The gender is in the question whether you meant it or not.
sentences.mnemonic: anti and ṭāliba both end in the light vowel — they travel together.

sentences.cue: No, I am a teacher (said by a woman)

words.note: Two jobs in one word. On its own it is the answer "no", as here. In front of a verb it is "not" — lā urīd, "I do not want" — which is how M3 will negate; Arabic needs no extra "do" to do it.
mudarris is a male teacher, mudarrisa a female one — the -a again follows whoever is being described. Literally "one who teaches", from darasa, to study.

sentences.trap: "No, I'm not" has nothing to translate to. Say no, then say what IS true.
sentences.sound: laa is a long open vowel. mu-DAR-ri-sa doubles the r.

variations.cue: No, I am a student (said by a woman)
variations.changed: the same no, a different fact after it

variations.cue: No, I am a teacher (said by a man)
variations.changed: drop the -a: a man describes himself as mudarris

variations.cue: Yes, I am a teacher (said by a woman)
variations.changed: the guess was right this time — naʿam, and the same fact confirms it

mistake.why: Said by a woman this is wrong: mudarris is the male teacher. She says anā mudarrisa.

sentences.usage: Correcting a wrong guess: no, and here is the right answer.
sentences.mnemonic: madrasa is a school and mudarris is the one who teaches in it.

sentences.cue: Do you like tea? (to a man)

words.note: shāy is tea. The article in front of it is al-, but sh is a sun letter, so the l is swallowed and the sh doubles: ash-shāy. This course spells it the way it is said — al-shāy is not another spelling of this word, it is no word at all. Liking tea in general keeps the article, exactly as al-qahwa did.

sentences.trap: English needs "do" to ask this. Arabic needs hal — and the verb keeps its tu- prefix, which is where the "you" lives.
sentences.sound: hal tu-ḤIBB ash-SHAAY — you can hear the doubled sh, and no l anywhere.

variations.cue: Do you like coffee? (to a man)
variations.changed: tea → coffee, and al- comes back in one piece: q is a moon letter
drop hal and change the prefix — the answer to the question

variations.cue: Do you like tea? (to a woman)
variations.changed: asked of a woman, the verb grows the -īn tail: tuḥibbīn — the prefix alone stops being enough

mistake.why: The l of al- never survives in front of sh. It is ash-shāy — said that way, and in this course written that way too.

sentences.usage: Offering and asking about likes. Tea is the default offer nearly everywhere Arabic is spoken.
sentences.mnemonic: shāy is chai with the same leaves in it — and al- disappears into the sh.

comprehensionPool.cue: Are you a student? (to a man)
Are you from India? (to a woman)
Do you like music? (to a man)
Good evening, how are you? (to a woman)
Are you a teacher? (to a man)
I am a teacher and I like tea (said by a man)
Do you like coffee? (to a woman)
